title: Two Planes Collide on the Ground in Miami; Only Minor Injuries Reported
summary:
Two planes bumped into each other on the ground at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, and two people reported minor injuries. The crash happened at about 9 p.m. at a taxiway intersection, where planes cross paths while moving around the airport. One plane was a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 carrying 172 people. The other was a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, which carries packages instead of passengers. The wingtip of the Copa plane struck the nose of the UPS plane. Photos from the scene show a long gash on one side of the UPS plane's nose and a larger hole in the middle.

Investigators say the UPS plane was told to give way to the Copa flight but did not stop. On a recording of the pilots' radio calls, the UPS pilot told air traffic control that he had gone too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The National Transportation Safety Board, which investigates aviation accidents, said the UPS aircraft had substantial damage. An assessment of the Copa plane had not been finished yet.

Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. 'We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,' UPS said in a statement. The company said the safety board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information. The safety board has opened an investigation and expects to release a first report within 30 days.
why_it_matters: Even slow collisions on the ground can injure people and damage planes, so the rules about who moves first at busy airport crossings matter for everyone's safety. The investigation's findings could change how pilots and controllers handle these crossings.

background_read: Airports have special roads called taxiways that planes use to move between runways and gates, and busy crossings need clear rules about who goes first.
Air traffic controllers guide planes from a tower, telling pilots when to move, wait, or give way to another plane.
When something goes wrong, the National Transportation Safety Board investigates to find out what happened and how to stop it happening again.
Even a slow bump on the ground can damage a plane, so investigators check both aircraft carefully before they fly again.
